body: CCing @gordthompson @jvanasco @CaselIT can we review the operators here, there is some precedent for SQLite regexp here: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/5071601/how-do-i-use-regex-in-a-sqlite-query/8338515#8338515  https://github.com/ralight/sqlite3-pcre  if we can see what they do, above all we need to add tests that check if each backend's regexp acts a search.

https://www.pcre.org/original/doc/html/pcre_exec.html  - "It returns offsets to captured substrings."   the above C library is not using any options which means the PCRE_ANCHORED flag is not set so it seems to support that the packaged use case for SQLite's regex acts like search.

yes, I agree we should use `search` instead of `match`. I guess we did kind of assumed match since it's called regexp matching everywhere.

@xflr6 would you like to provide a pr to fix this?

Thanks for the quick answer.

Feel free to go ahead (sounds like nice small fix, but I am not sure if I can find the time for it).

I've not started it, if you want to have a go at it feel free

**Federico Caselli** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **master** branch:

**Use ``re.search`` instead of ``re.match`` in sqlite** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/2365

Not sure if this was considered before: Would it make sense to use `is not None` instead of `bool()`?

```python
In [1]: import re

In [2]: %timeit bool(re.search(r'spam', 'eggs'))
1.24 µs ± 2.37 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1000000 loops each)

In [3]: %timeit re.search(r'spam', 'eggs') is not None
1.1 µs ± 5.09 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1000000 loops each)

In [4]: %timeit bool(re.search(r'spam', 'spam'))
1.4 µs ± 76.3 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1000000 loops each)

In [5]: %timeit re.search(r'spam', 'spam') is not None
1.2 µs ± 4.06 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1000000 loops each)
```
